title: Follow one request
summary: Trace a book search from a browser to a service and database, then follow the reply back. Find where a slow step adds waiting time.
introduction: Imagine asking the librarian where a book is. Your question travels to the desk, the librarian checks the catalog, and an answer comes back. A web request makes a similar round trip.
learningObjectives: Follow a request and its response
Describe the client, service, and database roles
Distinguish a failed request from an empty search result

blocks.text: A **request** asks another part to do work. A **response** is its reply. The browser is the client in this example. The library service checks the question and uses the database to find the answer.
The browser first needs the service address. **DNS** is a name lookup that helps find a network address for a name. With **HTTPS**, the connection uses encryption to protect data while it travels.
Some work may already be ready. The browser may remember a DNS answer for a time or reuse an open connection. Our trace starts after the connection is ready, so it can focus on the search.
The public browser should not receive database passwords. It sends a request to a carefully designed service instead of connecting directly to a private database.

items: The learner types Moon. The browser sends a search request.
The service checks that the search text and page size are allowed.
The service asks the database for a small page of matching records.
The database returns records. The service prepares a reply with only the needed fields.
The browser receives the reply and shows the titles and shelf labels.

blocks.alt: A book search goes from the browser to the book service and database. The result returns through the service to the browser.
blocks.caption: Read from top to bottom. The service and browser appear twice because this shows their actions during one round trip.

blocks.code:
Browser -> Service: GET /v1/books?title=moon&limit=2
Service: check the title and limit
Service -> Database: find matching book records
Database -> Service: book 17, title Moon, shelf B2
Service -> Browser: 200 OK with the result list
Browser: show Moon on shelf B2
blocks.title: Follow one request example

blocks.text: The arrows going back are as important as the arrows going out. A successful database lookup is not enough if the final reply never reaches the learner.
Each step adds some time. A slow database query, a busy service, or a slow network can delay the whole trip. Measure the steps before choosing where to improve the design.
No matching books is a valid answer: return a successful search with an empty list. A database that cannot answer is a different problem and needs a clear temporary-failure response.
A **timeout** is a waiting limit. If a needed part does not respond in time, stop waiting and show a useful message. An endless spinning symbol does not help the learner decide what to do.
A message can be lost on its way back. For a read, trying again is usually safe. Changing stored data needs extra care because the first attempt may already have worked.

items: Imagine the database has no book with the requested title. Change the trace after the database lookup.
The database returns an empty list. The service replies with success and an empty list; the page says No matching books. This is not the same as a broken connection.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not draw only the forward path. Follow the answer all the way back, including what the learner sees when a step fails.
